records.quote: differentially-private training typically prevents models from capturing the long tails of the data distribution and thus hurts utility [19, 20, 67].

records.claim: User-level DP models require labels for which users contributed each document, which are unavailable for data scraped from the open Web.
records.quote: this work requires labels for which users contributed each document; such labels are unavailable for data scraped from the open Web.

records.claim: It is unclear how to apply DP in a principled and effective way on Web data because rare snippets of text might appear in more than one webpage.
records.quote: It is thus unclear how to apply DP in a principled and effective way on Web data.

records.claim: Sanitizing data is imperfect and serves as a first line of defense rather than an outright prevention against privacy leaks.
records.quote: Overall, sanitizing data is imperfect—some private data will always slip through—and thus it serves as a first line of defense and not an outright prevention against privacy leaks.

records.claim: Fine-tuning LMs on task-specific data may cause the model to forget some data memorized during pre-training.
records.quote: On the positive side, this finetuning process may cause the LM to “forget” [42, 57] some of the data that is memorized during the pre-training stage.

records.claim: Fine-tuning may introduce its own privacy leakages if the task-specific data contains private information.
records.quote: On the negative side, fine-tuning may introduce its own privacy leakages if the task-specific data also contains private information.

records.claim: Auditing models is important even when using differential privacy as it can complement theoretical upper bounds on privacy leakage.
records.quote: Auditing is important even when using differential privacy, as it can complement theoretical upper bounds on privacy leakage [1].

records.claim: State-of-the-art LMs memorize their training data in practice, and adversaries can extract this data with simple techniques.
records.quote: Our results show that state-of-the-art LMs do memorize their training data in practice, and that adversaries can extract this data with simple techniques.

records.claim: The attacks are practical even when the data contains a given sequence only a few times.
records.quote: Our attacks are practical even when the data contains a given sequence only a few times.

records.claim: Among 600,000 generated samples, at least 604 (0.1%) contain memorized text.
records.quote: In particular, among 600,000 (honestly) generated samples, our attacks find that at least 604 (or 0.1%) contain memorized text.

records.claim: The finding of 604 memorized samples is likely an extremely loose lower bound because only 1,800 potential candidates were manually inspected.
records.quote: Note that this is likely an extremely loose lower bound. We only manually inspected 1,800 potential candidate memorized samples

records.claim: Preventing overfitting does not prevent models from memorizing training data, as large LMs have no significant train-test gap yet still memorize examples verbatim.
records.quote: However, large LMs have no significant train-test gap, and yet we still extract numerous examples verbatim from the training set.

records.claim: Memorization occurs because some training examples have anomalously low losses, even if the average training loss is only slightly lower than validation loss.
records.quote: The key reason is that even though on average the training loss is only slightly lower than the validation loss, there are still some training examples that have anomalously low losses.

records.claim: Larger language models consistently memorize more training data than smaller LMs.
records.quote: Throughout our experiments, larger language models consistently memorized more training data than smaller LMs.

records.claim: The 1.5 billion parameter GPT-2 model memorizes over 18 times as much content as the 124 million parameter model.
records.quote: For example, in one setting the 1.5 billion parameter GPT-2 model memorizes over $18 \times$ as much content as the 124 million parameter model

records.claim: Privacy leakage will likely become more prevalent as LMs become bigger.
records.quote: Worryingly, it is likely that as LMs become bigger (in fact they already are $100 \times$ larger than the GPT-2 model we study [7]), privacy leakage will become even more prevalent.

records.claim: Much of the extracted training data is only discovered when prompting the LM with a particular prefix.
records.quote: Much of the training data that we extract is only discovered when prompting the LM with a particular prefix.

records.claim: Mitigation strategies such as differential privacy, vetting data, limiting impact, and auditing are incomplete solutions to the memorization problem.
records.quote: All of these are interesting and promising avenues of future work, but each has weaknesses and are incomplete solutions to the full problem.

records.claim: Training Data Extraction Attack is practical and efficient, and can recover hundreds of training examples from a model, even when they are contained in just one training document.
records.quote: Our extraction attacks are practical and efficient, and can recover hundreds of training examples from a model, even when they are contained in just one training document.

records.claim: The techniques used in the Training Data Extraction Attack apply to any language model, not just GPT-2.
records.quote: Even though our attacks target GPT-2 (which allows us to ensure that our work is not harmful), the same techniques apply to any LM.

records.claim: Memorization gets worse as language models become larger, so vulnerabilities to extraction attacks will become significantly more important in the future.
records.quote: Moreover, because memorization gets worse as LMs become larger, we expect that these vulnerabilities will become significantly more important in the future.

records.claim: Training with differentially-private techniques is a method for mitigating privacy leakage, but new methods are necessary to train models at extreme scale without sacrificing accuracy or training time.
records.quote: Training with differentially-private techniques is one method for mitigating privacy leakage, however, we believe that it will be necessary to develop new methods that can train models at this extreme scale (e.g., billions of parameters) without sacrificing model accuracy or training time.

records.claim: A URL that is used (intentionally) only once can be included in the dataset tens of times due to the replies.
records.quote: As a result, a URL that is used (intentionally) only once can be included in the dataset tens of times due to the replies.
